content.thinking:
I'm sketching a whimsical capybara design—chubby and rounded with a barrel body, blunt snout, tiny ears, exaggerated slightly from its real ~1.2m size with a shorter-legged, chubbier look—plus a small bird companion perched on its head.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: a spine chain from hips to chest, neck, head, jaw, four legs with toes, a tiny tail stub, ears, and a separate bird rig (body, head, wings, tail, legs, beak) parented to the capybara's head joint. I'm planning the exact coordinates for each body part—body height around 0.8m total, with the barrel torso, legs, head, and bird stacked proportionally—working out rump, spine, chest, and neck positions along the z-axis for a smooth arched body sweep.

I should add a tiny tail nub joint since capybaras barely have a visible tail. I'm working out the body path points and how hips connects as the root joint feeding into the spine chain, trying to figure out the right starting coordinates so the rear and spine segments line up properly.

Now I'm mapping out the spine and neck joint chains, deciding how to parent the neck to the spine's end point and then attach a separate head joint at the neck's tip with its own aim direction.

For the body itself, I'm thinking of it as a loft running from hips to neck, laying out width/height stations at different z-positions from the butt (narrower) through the torso (widest around the midsection) up to the shoulders near the neck, to get a believable silhouette.

The neck tapers from a wider base down to about 0.13 radius before blending into the cheeks of the head, with a separate sweep for the neck chain that gets buried into the body loft for seamless skin.

For the legs, I'm making them short, stubby capybara-like columns with just a couple segments each (shoulder-to-foot for front legs, hip-to-foot for hind legs), using tube radii tapering from about .075 down to .045, and planning simple three-to-four-toed feet with small claw-like hooves.

Adding toe joints and leg chains...

I'll finalize names as shoulderFL/elbowFL/wristFL for the front leg chain, positioning the shoulder joint embedded into the body and angling the elbow back before the wrist drops down near the foot, with toes extending forward from there.

Each foot gets four toes as short rounded capsules resting flat on the floor with a slight sink for ground contact, plus a dark nail tip and a toe joint parented to the wrist. For the hind legs I'm setting up a bigger thigh with hip, knee (bent forward), and hock (bent back) joints leading down to the foot.

Now for the head I'm planning a loft-based skull shape — back of skull, forehead, then a boxy capybara snout with a big flat nose — using wider cross-sections to capture that distinctive stubby, blocky muzzle.

I'm planning the mouth and nose details: a slit mouth with overhanging upper lip, a dark flattened nose pad at the snout tip, and small dark nostril lumps positioned wide-set and upturned for that whimsical capybara look. For the eyes, I'm placing small glossy black spheres with white highlights high on the sides of the head, slightly enlarged for charm.

For a sleepy half-lidded effect, I'm adding a partial-sphere eyelid cap in coat color over each eye, tilted to give that chill capybara expression, plus pinkish cheek blush discs for extra whimsy.

I'm thinking through whiskers as thin dark rods near the nose, and sketching rounded dark ears with inner pink detail positioned at the top rear of the head.

For the fur, I'm settling on a warm brown-ochre coat with a lighter countershaded belly, using mottling for texture variation. I'll scatter around 120 small fur tuft cards across the cheeks, neck, chest, and rump for a shaggy whimsical look, shading them by facing direction.

For texture resolution I'm checking a 1024 sheet against the capybara's roughly 1.1m body gives about 2mm density, which should be plenty sharp. Then for fun story details, I'm adding a cheerful little bluebird perched on its head with an orange breast and yellow beak, maybe holding a tiny red berry, plus a small daisy tucked nearby for charm.

I'm settling on a daisy tucked behind the left ear and a blade of grass sticking out the corner of its slightly closed mouth, since capybaras munch grass — a nice whimsical touch without overcrowding with extras like butterflies or ladybugs.

Now I'm sketching the bird's rig perched on the capybara's head: a small body-to-head joint, beak upper/lower joints, two-segment wings and tail, and simple leg/foot joints with minimal rigid toe sticks rather than full articulated digits, sized to a tiny ~12cm songbird scale.

Continuing the bird's structure, I'm placing a head joint with a rounded sphere, orange-yellow beak cone, black dot eyes with highlights, pink cheek blush, and a tiny three-feather crest tuft. I'm planning folded wings as teardrop-shaped extrusions on each side with layered feather shading and darker wing tips, rigged with their own joints.

For the tail I'm fanning out three feather extrudes tilted upward from a tail joint, and adding tiny orange legs from the belly down to tiny clawed feet, mostly hidden by the breast. For coloring, I'm giving the bird a blue back with cream belly and orange-ish breast using countershading, plus wing bar stripes, and finishing the eyes with black spheres and white highlights. I'm also measuring the head's surface geometry to make sure the top of the skull aligns properly with the body.

Now I'm shooting a ray downward to find where the bird should sit on the skull, so I can root its feet and body at that contact point, with legs anchored to the hit location and the body offset slightly above. I'm parenting the bird's body joint to the head joint, then moving on to capybara details like whiskers near the snout and a dark mouth line sweeping from the snout to the cheek.

Working through nostril and teeth placement...

I'll position the upper buck teeth to poke slightly below the lip, opening the jaw a touch so they're visible without overlapping the lower jaw, keeping the rest pose neutral and closed. Then I'm thinking through jowl bulges with fur tufts on the cheeks, and adding subtle belly lightening and scattered darker freckle patches to the fur for texture.

Now I'm adding capybara-specific details: the morrillo scent gland as a dark hairless oval bump at the top of the snout, fuzzy hind legs with toenails, pink-and-dark ear interiors, and cheek fur tufts. I'm deciding against a base platform, bumping the head proportions larger (width .27, height .30) for a whimsical look with eyes at y=.56, and keeping the color palette limited to around 64 flat colors to stay manageable.

Drafting the full palette now — coat browns, belly tan, nose and eye darks, white and blush accents, grass greens, daisy colors, and blue/orange bird tones.

I'm thinking through how the fur tuft texture should be drawn: as a greyscale strand cluster that gets tinted at runtime via a color paint reading the part's root color, so the same atlas texture can serve any fur color.

Next I'm working out the grass blade in the bird's mouth — a tapered sweep shape attached to the jaw bone, curving from the mouth corner outward with a leaf-like cross-section that narrows to a point at the tip, using a width function that shrinks the radius toward the end for a natural taper.

For the daisy behind the ear, I'm deciding to place it on the head oriented along the surface normal, built as a ring of six petals around a yellow center disk, with each petal framed to aim outward and lean flat against the head like a flower lying on the surface rather than standing upright.

I'm adding a tucked leaf by the ear, small blush decals, sleepy curved eyebrows, and half-lidded whimsical eyes, then deciding to skip toon-kit shading since it's not needed for this style. Now starting the actual code, beginning with the body skeleton using a hips joint as the root.

Still writing joint hierarchy...

I'm finishing the body loft at z .46, merging into the neck, and checking the bone chain hips-spine-neck lines up with those stations. Checking the belly clearance against the legs, I realize the body is coming out taller than planned, so I'm scaling back the height and width to keep the whimsical capybara proportions closer to the back/head level.

Adjusting the y-center down slightly so the top sits near .59-.64 with visible leg clearance around .15-.17, and placing the head so it carries up above the back naturally. I'm rounding the barrel shape using about 10 sides for a softer silhouette, keeping the rump round, and positioning front legs at ±0.17 and hind legs at ±0.19 relative to the body's half-width.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry — tapering radii from shoulder to foot, deciding on coordinate conventions so left/right sides map correctly to model space, and sketching a simple polyline path for the front leg joints from shoulder to elbow to foot.

I'm naming the joints with side suffixes like shoulderFL, elbowFL, and wristFL, with wrist serving as the tip where the foot and toe chains attach — four toes in front, three in back.

Now I'm positioning the foot pad as a scaled sphere beneath the wrist, then adding toe capsules spreading forward with tapered radii and rounded caps, plus tiny dark nail spheres at the tips. I'm checking the vertical math so toes and pad sit flush with the floor without sinking more than a couple percent of body height, then moving on to define the hind leg's hip and knee joint positions.

Letting the haunch ride on the hip joint naturally as the leg bends, then adding a small tail chain parented to the hips with a short two-point sweep. Now I'm defining the head loft, starting with cranium and cheek cross-sections along the skull bone.

For the snout, I need to account for how round end caps extend past the final loft station by their own radius — so I'm adjusting the last station's position and size inward so the blunt capybara nose doesn't overshoot where I want the muzzle tip to land.

Looking at the rear station too: a round start cap on the head will poke a dome shape backward into the neck junction, possibly bulging above the withers where the neck is narrower than the head's base radius. A flat cap might look cleaner there, but it could show as a visible disc where the neck doesn't fully cover it — I need to check whether the neck radius is wide enough to hide that seam.

I'll adjust the head start station position and dimensions with rounded end caps, then add jowl spheres on the cheeks for a whimsical look. For the lower jaw, I'm sketching a tapered capsule shape running from the jaw joint forward, with flattened rounded ends to suggest a mouth.

Checking the vertical alignment: the jaw needs to sit below the upper snout rather than overlapping it, so I'm lowering its center y and shrinking its ry so the jaw protrudes just beneath the snout and cheek mass without colliding with them.

Adjusting the head loft stations so each successive slice narrows and lifts slightly, giving the cheeks their widest point mid-head and tapering toward the snout tip while keeping the bottom profile clear of the floor.

I'm realizing the head is coming out proportionally too large versus the body—nearly half the body length when a capybara head should be closer to a quarter—so I need to pull the starting z back and compress the dome-to-snout span, planning to preview and iterate rather than nail it analytically. I'm also considering swapping the snout's end cap from round to flat, possibly layering a nose pad sphere on top to get that blunt, squared-off capybara snout look instead of a pointed taper.

I need to figure out eye placement on the skull surface using a ray cast from the side to find the hit point and normal, then offset slightly inward to position the eye sphere there. For the eye itself, I'm planning a small colored sphere with a white highlight sphere layered on top for shine.

For the eyelid, I'm shaping a partial sphere cap slightly larger than the eye, oriented to tilt outward and cover the top portion, leaving the eye visible through the bottom opening like a sleepy lid. I'm also considering adding eyebrows for extra character.

Now I'm placing the nose pad on the front of the snout with a flattened ellipsoid shape, plus two small darker nostril holes positioned symmetrically, and sketching a seam line for the mouth that traces down from the nose along the lower edge of the snout using surface-snapped points to avoid floating geometry.

Then I'm adding small teeth boxes tucked under the upper jaw and considering whether to add lower jaw teeth too (likely skipping for simplicity), followed by placing tapered whisker spikes on each side of the snout, angled outward with thin radii.

Now I'm placing a dark oval scent bump on top of the muzzle using a ray-hit position, then working out ear geometry—trying a flattened sphere or an extruded teardrop outline tilted outward from the skull surface normal at the crown.

I'm setting up the ear hinge joint and planning an inner-ear detail plus small fur tuft, then thinking through fur cards scattered across the body surface with a tinted coat paint using mottled base color and layered grain streaks for texture variation.

Working out the fur paint blend between mottle and grain layers, with countershading for the belly and a darker gradient for the muzzle area on the head.

For the legs I'll darken toward the feet with a simple gradient. I'm also considering adding whimsical touches—blush decals on the cheeks using soft overlapping ellipses—applied onto the head loft once I confirm the skull geometry supports decal placement.

For the eyes, I'm weighing a 3D sphere approach against a flat SVG decal with iris, highlight, and lash details; I'll likely keep the 3D sphere for depth but may add a thin dark lash arc above as an accent, skipping that for now. I still need to compute the ray hit on the skull top to position features, and I'm sketching out the bird's body proportions—a chubby sphere sized relative to that hit point, facing forward along the same axis as the main figure.

Now I'm laying out the bird's structural chain, loft stations running from tail to neck with varying width and height to give it a plump shape, then setting up joints so the bird root attaches to the capybara's head and a separate bird chain handles the body and head segments.

Working on the head, beak, and eye details now — a small sphere for the head, spike-shaped cones for upper and lower beak parented to a jaw joint, tiny dark eye spheres with white highlights, and blush circles on the cheeks.

Now I'm adding a crest of small curved feathers using sweep geometry, then setting up the wing joints at the shoulders. I'm figuring out how to extrude a teardrop-shaped folded wing outline along the body flank, working through the orientation so it mirrors correctly on both sides.

Mapping out the wing outline points and layering a second darker extrude for the primary feathers, then painting feather stripes across the wing with coverts in blue and darker tips near the primaries.

Now I'm planning the tail as three fanned-out feather extrudes tilted upward, attached via a rigid joint on the spine tip, and sketching the legs as small orange sticks with a two-point chain for hip and foot plus toe sticks, positioned so they partly tuck under the plump belly.

I'm computing the body height so the bird sits properly above the head, with short stubby legs and three thin forward-gripping toes resting on the curved head surface, and considering tilting the head joint slightly to one side for a whimsical look before building anything attached to it.

I decide to keep the bird simple without extra accessories, then move to scattering fur cards across the body surface with set density, lean, and bend parameters, filtering out cards on the underside.

I add smaller cheek tufts with their own scatter pass, tint the fur using the coat color paint, and skip extras like eyelashes, tongue interior, or toenails to keep things clean—the triangle budget stays comfortably under control.

For a whimsical touch, I'm adding a grass blade poking out the left mouth corner, curling forward and slightly upward; I need to check the snout's surface width at that point so the curve starts properly outside the head rather than clipping into it, using a ray cast against the skull to find the correct anchor point before building the path and weighting it to the head bone.

I'm shaping the blade as a tapered ribbon with elliptical cross-section, adding a second smaller blade alongside it, coloring both with a grass gradient, and then moving on to body details like a lighter belly, chin/throat highlights, and eyebrow tufts before writing the actual builder code.

Writing imports and setup...

Adding more paint gradients for the face and legs, then sketching the fur tuft SVG with simple curved strand shapes...

Now I'm noting the build order — skull needs to exist before the bird and decal layers are added, with cards placed afterward, and setting the loft section sides count to 10.

I'm deciding on texture atlas resolution, leaning toward 1024 initially for crisp fur detail before considering 2048. Then I start laying out the skeleton joints, beginning with the hips joint and a spine chain built from catmull control points.

Still writing skeleton joints...

Still defining body loft...

Continuing the station layout, I worry the end cap near z .46-.64 pokes out past the head width at that height, so I shrink it to w .30 h .32 which keeps the dome within the head boundary. I'll move on to finalize all stations and iterate with the preview before tackling legs and the bird shape.

Building the front leg chain, attaching it to the spine's third joint near z~.2, naming the joints shoulder/elbow/wrist and sweeping tapered radii down to the foot.

Adding toe chains and sweeping them with the toe color...

Now I'm positioning a blunt nail sphere at each toe tip, keeping it flat and hoof-like like real capybara nails, then moving to the hind legs with three toes and a haunch sphere, working out the leg path so the lower leg slants backward from knee to ankle and the foot angles forward for a digitigrade stance, parented from the hips.

Adjusting haunch and shoulder sphere scale and placement against the body's width to make sure they bulge naturally outside the torso silhouette without clipping, checking the countershade coat paint still reads correctly on these scaled spheres.

I'm skipping the shoulder bump in favor of an elbow bump, then building the skull using a loft through several shaped cross-sections from the brow to the snout, with flat caps so I can later attach a flattened nose pad onto the front face.

Now I'm setting up the head joint at the neck, placing cheek jowls as scaled spheres rigged to the head bone, and sketching the jaw as a swept path with tapering radii so I can shade it lighter near the chin using a gradient derived from the belly tone.

I'm checking the overlap between the jaw and upper snout: the jaw spans roughly .325-.405 in height, visible only below .37, giving a modest chin of about 4.5cm, and its width needs to stay narrower than the skull's half-width for a believable profile.

Now I'm moving on to finalize details like a flatter skull bottom, eyes, and blush decals, then drafting the bird anchor logic—computing a crown hit point via a ray cast, deriving a base y-offset, and setting up the bird's joint hierarchy with spine roles for rigging.

Still writing joint positions...

Writing bird coloring logic...

Still defining beak spikes and jaw joint...

Now I'm placing the eyes as small dark spheres with offset white highlight spheres facing outward and upward on each side of the head.

For cheek blush, I'm considering using ellipsoid-shaped pink discs positioned just outside the head sphere's surface, and thinking about using a surface-based positioning helper (azimuth/elevation around the head sphere's center) to consistently place both the eyes and blush spots.

Now I'm working out the crest, using three bezier feather sweeps starting at the top of the head that curl back and upward, with tapering radii and the dark bird color on the head bone. Then I'm moving to the wing joints, figuring out their attachment point on the spine.

Writing wing outline coordinates...

Then I'll set up the tail joint parented to the spine, angled back and down, with three fanned leaf-shaped feather extrudes.

Now I'm working out the bird's legs as a two-point chain from spine to foot, with a thin orange sweep radius, then adding toes as forward/back sticks attached at the foot tip, positioning the foot by raycasting onto the head's crown surface.

I'm also figuring out placement for a daisy near the left ear and the ear itself, raycasting down onto the skull to find base positions, then estimating offsets in x and z to tuck the daisy between the bird and the ear without overlapping.

Still placing petals...

I'll orient the petal's thin axis toward the normal using the up direction, with a flattened yellow sphere at center for the flower core, plus a couple tiny green leaves behind it. Then I'm moving on to scattering fur cards across the body surface with minimum distance spacing.

Adding cheek tufts next, smaller cards filtered to the head area for a "mutton chops" look, while skipping chest ruff, leg fur, and back midline hair for simplicity. I'll also skip eyelash decals but consider adding a dark brow accent.

Now I'm working out the ear geometry: parenting the ear joint to the head, computing the hit direction, and extruding the outline with a thickness vector derived from a cross product so the ear faces front-to-back correctly. I'll add a slightly smaller pink inner-ear extrusion inset from the outer shape.

Next I'm figuring out eye placement by casting rays against the skull surface to find positions, offsetting into sockets, placing eye spheres with the correct radius and color, then adding highlight spheres offset toward a light direction for the glossy catchlight.

For the eyelid, I'm building it as a partial sphere covering the top portion of the eyeball, shaded darker than the coat color, deciding the opening angle so the globe stays visibly peeking through without worrying about the hidden underside.

Now I'm moving to facial details: a brow sweep above the eye, a nose pad as a flattened part-sphere with proportions scaled against the face width, dark nostril ellipsoids with a small highlight, and a draped mouth line using a catmull curve with a slight lift.

I'm building the full mouth polyline across both sides of the face so it drapes symmetrically onto the skull, then moving on to whisker placement, raycasting from points near the nose outward to find skull hits and spiking whisker geometry off those points with varying angles per row.

For teeth, I'm placing small box geometries along the jawline near the snout's bottom edge, though I'm noticing the positioning might cause them to protrude oddly relative to where the jaw's rounded front cap extends past the snout face — something to reconcile as I refine the proportions.

Now I'm designing a blush decal as a small SVG with layered gradient ellipses for the cheek tint, then figuring out how to project it onto the skull mesh using a hit point and outward normal direction for placement and sizing.
